sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
Feedback can turn from negative to positive if the loop adds enough phase shift. At the frequency where \(|T| = 1\), if the loop phase has reached \(-180^\circ\), a signal returns the same size and inverted twice (once by the loop, once by the subtraction). It sustains itself: the circuit oscillates.

A single-pole loop can never get there; it maxes out at \(-90^\circ\). Real op-amps have **non-dominant poles** at higher frequencies that add more lag. **Phase margin** measures how far from \(-180^\circ\) the loop phase is at crossover. Small margins give ringing and overshoot; about \(60^\circ\) is a good design target. Heavier feedback (larger \(f\), e.g. a unity-gain buffer) pushes crossover higher, closer to those extra poles, so it is the hardest case.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ PM = 180^\circ + \angle T(j\omega_c), \qquad |T(j\omega_c)| = 1 \]
Two-pole loop:
\[ T(j\omega) = \frac{T_0}{(1 + j\omega/\omega_1)(1 + j\omega/\omega_2)} \]
If \(\omega_c\) lands at the second pole \(\omega_2\), the phase is about \(-135^\circ\), giving \(PM \approx 45^\circ\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
A loop has a dominant pole far below crossover and a second pole at \(\omega_2\). Suppose crossover is at \(\omega_c = 0.5\,\omega_2\). The dominant pole gives nearly \(-90^\circ\), the second gives \(-\tan^{-1}(0.5) \approx -26.6^\circ\):
\[ \angle T \approx -116.6^\circ, \qquad PM \approx 63^\circ \]
That meets the \(60^\circ\) target.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Calling a phase of \(-180^\circ\) unstable without checking \(|T|\) there.
- Measuring phase margin at the closed-loop bandwidth instead of loop crossover.
- Assuming a buffer (gain 1) is the safest configuration; it has the most loop gain.
- Forgetting that a right-half-plane pole means instability regardless of margin.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Compensation, the deliberate creation of a dominant pole, is how op-amps guarantee stability. This is why their open-loop response looks single-pole over the useful range.
